extracted.intended_audience: state environmental agencies, regulated power-sector entities (utilities/plant operators), environmental and energy lawyers, and rulemaking stakeholders/commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal/technical criteria for selecting the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) and degrees of emission limitation for steam-generating units and stationary combustion turbines under CAA section 111, including subcategory-specific determinations and legal defenses (e.g., MQD).

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER: routine operation and maintenance for base/intermediate natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA is finalizing BSER for intermediate and base load natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units as routine methods of operation and maintenance, such that the sources could maintain the emission rates (on a lb/MWh-gross basis) currently maintained by the majority of the fleet across discrete ranges of annual capacity factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: units already operate with those practices; no or negligible additional costs; no change in required technology or operations; no adverse non-air health/environmental impacts or adverse long-term energy-sector impacts. Purpose: prevents increases in unit-level emission rates (no CO2 reductions at unit level, but maintains current performance). Applicability: finalized for intermediate and base load units regardless of operating horizon.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER: uniform fuels for low-load natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units
rubrics_metrics.description: For low load natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units, the EPA is finalizing a BSER of 'uniform fuels' with an associated presumptive standard of performance based on a heat input basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: high variability in emission rates at low loads makes lb CO2/MWh-gross standards unsuitable; heat-input (lb CO2/MMBtu) fuel-composition limits provide a reasonable presumptive standard. Presumptive degrees of limitation: fixed 130 lb CO2/MMBtu for natural gas-fired steam generating units and 170 lb CO2/MMBtu for oil-fired steam generating units. Related precedent: analogous to 2015 NSPS 'clean fuels' heat-input based fuel composition BSER for multi-fuel turbines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of emission limitation for base/intermediate natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units
rubrics_metrics.description: Because BSER is routine operation and maintenance (which units already employ), the degree of emission limitation is no increase in emission rate on a lb CO2/MWh-gross basis over an extended period of time (e.g., a year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This degree of limitation aims to maintain current fleet emission rates; it does not require additional control technologies or net CO2 reductions at the unit level, but is intended to prevent backsliding in GHG performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat Rate Improvements (HRI) are not BSER for steam generating units
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is not finalizing HRI as part of the BSER for any subcategory of existing steam generating units because HRI yields relatively minor overall GHG reductions and may cause a rebound effect that increases emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HRI measures include boiler-island improvements (neural network systems, intelligent sootblowers), turbine overhauls/upgrades, and equipment upgrades (variable frequency drives). Typical unit-level CO2 reductions from HRI range ~0.1–5% (most measures <1%; average reductions lower fleet-wide). Many HRI measures already applied at units or not broadly applicable; multiple HRI measures do not necessarily add cumulatively. Some measures affect net-generation (parasitic load) rather than gross-basis emission rates. Rebound risk: efficiency gains can lower operating costs and increase utilization, offsetting rate-based CO2 reductions. Because of small average reductions and rebound potential, HRI not selected as BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: CCS qualifies as BSER for long-term coal-fired steam generating units
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA determined carbon capture and storage (CCS)—a traditional add-on emissions control—is the BSER for long-term coal-fired steam generating units because it is adequately demonstrated, of reasonable cost, and achieves substantial emissions reductions (e.g., ~90% CO2 capture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal/technical rationale: CCS is an add-on control focused on individual-source performance (not system-wide generation shifting). EPA applied CAA §111(a)(1) factors (adequate demonstration, costs of control, and emissions reductions) in concluding CCS meets BSER criteria. Modeling and economic factors (including IRC section 45Q tax credits) affect adoption and dispatch; EPA explains retirements in modeling are consistent with historical trends and not evidence of impermissible 'generation-shifting.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with West Virginia v. EPA and the Major Questions Doctrine (MQD)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluations of BSER must account for the Supreme Court's West Virginia v. EPA and the MQD: a rule is permissible where BSER is a 'traditional' add-on control focused on improving performance of individual sources rather than an unprecedented generation-shifting program that transforms the statute's scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application: EPA analyzes whether a candidate BSER constitutes traditional pollution control (e.g., fuel-switching, add-on controls like CCS) vs. system-wide generation-shifting. The Agency documents statutory text (CAA §111) and historical practice, applies the statutory BSER factors, and compares modeling 'policy case' vs 'base case' to demonstrate impacts are incidental to controls and consistent with market/retirement trends. MQD concern is mitigated by showing BSER is add-on and authorized by Congress (including legislative history and later statutes like IRA/LEEP).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of co-firing (40% natural gas) standards — 'redefining the source' test
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA rejects the claim that a 40 percent natural gas co-firing performance standard unlawfully 'redefines the source'; fuel-switching/co-firing standards can be traditional pollution-control measures authorized under the CAA and Congress's amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: West Virginia's concern referenced complete repowering to 100% gas, not partial co-firing; 40% co-firing typically requires at most minor boiler changes and many units already co-fire at significant levels. Historical and statutory precedent supports fuel-switching standards. EPA cites data showing many units consume natural gas or have co-fired at >40% in at least one year; thus standards based on co-firing are practicable and not a forbidden redefinition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory review commitment and monitoring of technology/market developments
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA commits to review and, if appropriate, revise the rule by January 1, 2041, based on monitoring developments (e.g., IRC section 45Q tax credit expiration, CO2 utilization market growth, reductions in CCS operational costs, state decarbonization requirements, utility plans, SMR deployment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: permit reconsideration in light of changing economics, technological advances, and market supports that could materially affect the costs and viability of compliance options (e.g., continued operation with CCS after tax-credit expiration). EPA will consult other agencies (DOE), stakeholders, and track market developments to inform the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER determinations for new/reconstructed stationary combustion turbine EGUs (subcategories)
rubrics_metrics.description: For stationary combustion turbine EGUs commencing construction or reconstruction after May 23, 2023 (40 CFR part 60, subpart TTTTa), EPA finalizes BSER and standards for three subcategories: low load, intermediate load, and base load turbines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low load turbines: BSER = use of lower-emitting fuels (heat-input based fuel composition). Intermediate load turbines: BSER = highly efficient simple cycle generation. Base load turbines: BSER includes two components corresponding initially to a two-phase standard of performance (details codified in subpart TTTTa). EPA explains technology distinctions (simple cycle vs combined cycle) and how subcategories are applied; the preamble cross-references sections VIII.F and VIII.G for specific standards and rationale.
